entry.evidence: Well-established relative homogenization methods developed for temperature and precipitation exist but have rarely been applied to snow-cover-related time series.

sequences.source_document: Published paper (XML text, PDF for figures)

steps.action: Posed five research questions: which method or set-up works, elevation dependence, consistency with metadata, homogeneity of the network, and similarity across snow variables.
steps.quote: Which method or set-up works for break point detection in (Swiss) snow depth time series?

steps.action: Compiled manually measured Swiss snow depth series from MeteoSwiss and SLF archives, selected 184 series by length and completeness, and derived annual HSavg and dHS1.
steps.quote: Applying these criteria resulted in a data set of 184 station time series

steps.action: Compiled station-history metadata (coordinate changes as a relocation proxy, observer changes) from records, archives, and databases, to be used as verification within ±2 years.
steps.quote: Metadata are therefore used as additional verification for the identified break points

steps.action: Configured three relative homogenization tools: HOMER pairwise detection in Ratio-mode with a 0.8 correlation threshold and 3-of-5 rule, ACMANTv4.3 in precipitation mode, and Climatol with elevation weighting and SNHT thresholds set from its exploratory analysis.
steps.quote: we used Ratio-mode instead of differences

steps.action: Defined valid break points as those detected by at least two of three methods within ±2 years, independent of metadata, and planned comparisons with elevation, mean HSavg, and station history.
steps.quote: at least two out of three independent methods within a tolerance of ± 2 years regardless of metadata

steps.action: Ran each method on HSavg and counted the detected break points by method and decade: ACMANT 170 in 98 series, Climatol 61 in 54, HOMER 32 in 30.
steps.quote: Here we found ACMANT returning the largest number of detected break points with 170 breaks in 98 of the 184 series.

steps.action: Compared the methods' break magnitude correction distributions (histograms and density plots), finding that ACMANT detects many low-magnitude breaks and HOMER fewer, larger ones.
steps.quote: ACMANT detects the most break points, including those of lower magnitude, whereas HOMER identifies fewer but higher-magnitude breaks

steps.action: Stated the hypothesis that low-elevation stations lack enough suitable reference series for proper break detection.
steps.quote: To test the hypothesis that lower stations might not have enough suitable reference series for proper break point detections

steps.action: Compared break magnitude corrections with station elevation and climatological HSavg: fewer breaks below 500 and above 1800 m, no clear pattern with HSavg, and similar patterns across all three methods.
steps.quote: found fewer break points below 500 and above 1800 m a.s.l. than between 1300 and 1700 m a.s.l.

steps.action: Applied the two-of-three consensus to the single-method detections, yielding 31 valid HSavg breaks in 30 series (83% of series homogeneous), mostly from the ACMANT-HOMER combination, and computed each method's efficiency.
steps.quote: This approach identified 31 break points in 30 series for HSavg

steps.action: Checked the valid breaks against the station history: 22 of 31 were supported (19 relocations, 3 observer changes) and 11 had no metadata support.
steps.quote: 22 of the 31 detected break points were supported by metadata

steps.action: Repeated the whole detection and consensus procedure on a second variable, days with snow cover (dHS1), finding 20 valid breaks that are on average smaller (5% versus 14%).
steps.quote: The same procedures as outlined in Sect. 4.1 and 4.2 above were applied to another important and commonly used snow indicator

steps.action: Because only 6 of 45 breaks agree between the two variables, refined the assessment into a complementary HSavg plus dHS1 approach.
steps.quote: Six (out of 45) of the break points (13 %) agree, indicating that a complementary approach may be beneficial

steps.action: Varied method settings: lowering Climatol's SNHT thresholds changed the number of breaks, and running ACMANT on 188 instead of 184 series shifted some break years by up to ±2 years.
steps.quote: if using 188 instead of 184 series, the break points for some stations shifted slightly

steps.action: Tested the reference-series hypothesis by analysing HOMER ratio-series noise (sigma) and median correlations against altitude; noise is higher below 800 and above 1800 m, consistent with sparse references (supplement Figs. S2 and S3).
steps.quote: The higher noise (due to not enough suitable reference series being available) associated with these lower (and upper) stations may explain the different results

steps.action: Compared method sensitivity ordering and break magnitude distributions with Coll et al. (2020) for Irish precipitation and found them similar.
steps.quote: are similar to the ones found by working on Irish precipitation series

steps.action: Kept the method verdict: HOMER has the highest efficiency as a single method, but a combination of the three methods works best for snow series.
steps.quote: We found rather that a combination of the three methods works best

steps.action: Drew from the authors' earlier work the expectation that the more variable HSavg should show larger breaks than dHS1, offset by higher noise.
steps.quote: The larger variability associated with HSavg when compared to dHS1 would be expected to lead to larger breaks

steps.action: Inserted the dHS1-detected breaks into HSavg in HOMER and found the corrections no different from HSavg-only breaks; found dHS1 amplitudes smaller and dHS1 capturing most breaks below 1000 m.
steps.quote: Break magnitude corrections retrieved from HOMER using breaks detected in dHS1 and inserted into HSavg do not differ

steps.action: Compared all 519 recorded location changes with the valid breaks; only 45 (9%) produced a valid break, so metadata are not sufficient for verification.
steps.quote: only 45 relocated stations (9 %) produced a valid break point across all three methods

steps.action: Compared the inhomogeneity fractions and method agreement with Marcolini et al. (2017, 2019) and Schöner et al. (2019): similar numbers with the complementary approach, fewer with HSavg alone.
steps.quote: We found similar numbers: 17 % as inhomogeneous time series when only HSavg breaks are considered

steps.action: Kept the homogeneity assessment: 45 valid breaks in 41 of 184 series, 71% explained by metadata and 88% of those by relocation, with the multi-method, two-variable configuration recommended.
steps.quote: We identified 45 valid break points in 41 of 184 (22 %) series investigated using a complementary approach of HSavg and dHS1

end.claim: Using a two-of-three-method consensus within ±2 years on HSavg and dHS1, 45 valid break points occur in 41 of 184 Swiss snow depth series (22%), 71% of them explained by metadata and mostly by station relocation.

decisive_move.sentence: The two-of-three-method consensus filter turned 263 single-method detections into the 31 (later 45) valid break points on which every headline number rests.

gates.evidence: Action: the data were archival series compiled before any hypothesis, and the only stated hypothesis (elevation, §4.1.3 ¶1) came at the analysis stage. Claim: breaks could have failed the two-of-three consensus and the metadata check (22 of 31 supported). There is no truth benchmark, so detection and false-alarm rates cannot be assessed (§5.4 ¶2). Registration: nothing is reported as fixed before seeing the data. Climatol SNHT thresholds were 'Determined by expl-results' on the same data (Table 1), and the ±2-year tolerance and 5-year edge rule were adopted from prior studies.

imports.item: Penalized likelihood change-point criterion and optimal segmentation by dynamic programming (Caussinus and Lyazrhi 1997; Hawkins 2001) underlying HOMER/PRODIGE
Joint segmentation of multiple CGH profiles (Picard et al. 2011, Biostatistics), available in HOMER but not used
R 4.1.1 environment used to run HOMER and Climatol

novelty_claims.quote: We present the first in-depth break point detection comparison of three homogenization methods for snow depth time series.
[...] present the first detailed homogeneity assessment of Swiss snow depth series using state-of-the-art homogenization methods
the approach combining multiple methods introduced here for application to snow depth series is more rigorous

limits: No review file or open-discussion record was supplied. The paper was in open discussion from 17 March 2022 and thanks three referees, so no review sequence is coded and the effect of review on the text is unknown. True break points are unknown and no snow benchmark exists (§5.1 ¶5, §5.4 ¶2), so method performance is characterized only relative to inter-method consensus, not against truth. The Climatol thresholds were tuned on the same data (Table 1), and the paper does not say whether other set-ups were tried and discarded beyond the qualitative threshold remarks (§5.1 ¶2); inference: the reported configuration is one of several explored ('experimenting with various configurations', §1 ¶4). Sub-claims and their statuses: (a) HOMER is the best single method and the three-method combination works best, capability_characterized, but only relative to consensus; (b) station relocation is the main cause of breaks, best_explanation, limited by incomplete metadata (§5.3 ¶1); (c) fewer detections at low and high elevations are due to sparse or noisy reference series, best_explanation, with Figs. S2 and S3 not seen by the coder; (d) dHS1 breaks can be used to correct HSavg, regularity_in_range, on six shared breaks only. Internal tensions in the text: §4.2 ¶1 describes concordant breaks as 'identified across all three methods' but applies a two-of-three rule. §5.3 ¶1 says HOMER and Climatol return the highest proportion of valid breaks, while Table 2 gives Climatol 28% against HOMER 72% for HSavg. V checks performed here are method, control and robustness. Comparisons with Schöner et al. (2019), Marcolini et al. and Coll et al. (2020) are coded as cited, not performed here. Under that coding, no two performed checks differ in kind among replication, method and generalization, so triangulation is not met.

disagreements.target: Coll et al. (2020) recommendation of Climatol for precipitation series
disagreements.support: In the Swiss snow network HOMER had the highest efficiency (72% versus 28% for Climatol and 18% for ACMANT, Table 2), and the multi-method combination performed best.
disagreements.quote: our analysis shows that this might not be the same when applied to snow series in a more [...]

disagreements.target: Marcolini et al. (2019): 45% agreement between SNHT and PRODIGE for Austrian snow depth
disagreements.support: Here the analogous pair, Climatol (SNHT-based) and HOMER (PRODIGE-based), agreed on only 20% of breaks.
disagreements.quote: We only found 20 % (25 % for HSavg and 16 % for dHS1) agreement between Climatol and HOMER.

disagreements.target: Previous snow homogeneity studies (Marcolini et al. 2017, 2019; Schöner et al. 2019)
disagreements.support: Inhomogeneity numbers are similar with the complementary approach but lower for HSavg alone, which the authors attribute to the multi-method consensus and strict criteria.
disagreements.quote: if we only compare the break points found in HSavg, our results show fewer break points than have been identified by the previous studies

disagreements.target: Kuglitsch et al. (2012): Swiss temperature breaks explained by a combination of reasons
disagreements.support: Metadata attribute 19 of 22 supported HSavg breaks, and 88% of explained breaks overall, to relocation.
disagreements.quote: whereas our results tend to indicate that station relocation is the most likely source of inhomogeneities for the snow series analysed
